source.title: Shared Latent Structures Enable Unified Backdoor Detection and Mitigation in LLMs
source.authors: Omar Mahmoud; Aly M. Kassem; T. G. Karimpanal; Buddhika Laknath Semage; Negar Rostamzadeh; Golnoosh Farnadi; Santu Rana

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some table content is flattened in the supplied text, making some cell assignments unclear.
record.tranche_reason: The paper applies SAE feature discovery and interventions to LLM backdoors and reports results on real models. This extends the indirect SAE-feature evidence in V4 to a new setting; it does not test toy-model superposition geometry.
record.gate_note: The paper reports SAE-based feature detection and interventions, including activation steering and training-time ablation. Results from cited work are not included. Some per-feature values in Table 1, and more granular values in Table 8, are flattened and not safely assignable; the main-text results and the clearly aligned aggregate Table 3 are recorded instead.
record.test_reason: The study uses pretrained SAEs as a tool to find backdoor-related features, then reports how well its own detection, steering and CAFT methods work. It assumes residual streams 'may encode concepts in superposition' but never tests it. It does not measure feature spread across neurons, SAE recovery quality, toy geometry, capacity, canonicality or dimensionality. The backdoors are also implanted on purpose. None of its results bear on whether any version holds.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct: many backdoors share a recurring SAE-feature subspace that can be detected, steered and ablated during training. The subspace is not universal: weight-edited, some refusal, and inductive backdoors transfer weakly or use other mechanisms.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses SAE model diffing, activation steering, detection classifiers, and Concept Ablation Fine-Tuning on LLM backdoors. It does not reproduce the toy-network feature-geometry method or measure its sparsity-dependent geometric transition.
record.method_sensitivity: Transfer and mitigation vary by backdoor type and attack mechanism; password-locking has inverted steering polarity, weight-edited sentiment transfer is weaker, and refusal backdoors are harder to suppress. Outcomes also depend on SAE quality, layer coverage, sparsity structure, and dictionary size, as noted by the authors.

fits_no_version.finding: SAE decoder directions gave stronger bidirectional steering control of implanted backdoors than residual-stream mean-difference or probe directions (Tables 1, 2).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sparse dictionary directions give more precise causal handles on fine-tuning-induced behaviours than dense residual directions.

record.problems: The authors report that the shared subspace is not universal and that some attack types transfer weakly or use alternative mechanisms. SAE quality, layer coverage, sparsity structure, and dictionary size may affect results. Detection is evaluated in controlled clean-versus-triggered settings, and steering and CAFT need further testing at larger scales and against adaptive adversaries. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the listed outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Some per-feature outcomes in Table 1 and per-behavior detector scores in Appendix Table 8 were not extracted because the supplied flattened text does not safely preserve all cell-to-row assignments. Figure 3 includes additional model-by-behavior CAFT values; only the explicit numerical examples and weaker case described in the main text were recorded.

untested.parts: All of it: no toy models, sparsity transition or geometry.
All of it: no capacity analysis.
All of it: no neuron-level polysemanticity analysis.
All of it: SAEs are used as a tool; there is no measure of feature spread across neurons or of SAE recovery of the model's features.
All of it: no test of completeness, stability or canonicality.
All of it: no test of feature dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: The study is a backdoor-defence paper that uses SAEs instrumentally. Superposition is only invoked as the motivation for using SAEs (Sec. 3.1). The reader's V4 labels conflated the study's method performance with evidence for superposition and should be dropped.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks, feature sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular overlap geometry.
Whether polysemanticity results from competition for limited capacity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.

The study tests SAE-recoverable features associated with backdoor behaviors, not whether ordinary LLM features generally spread across neurons or whether the recovered features explain general model representations.
Feature completeness, stability, and canonicality across dictionaries, layers, or training runs.
Whether the represented features are intrinsically one-dimensional rather than multidimensional.

rows.subject: Qwen3-8B
rows.operation_detail: Evaluated shared SAE features on an inductive backdoor and examined features specific to that backdoor.
rows.measure: shared-feature activation and mitigation; specialized-feature control
rows.value: Shared features neither activate strongly nor reliably mitigate the behavior; two specialized features consistently control it and are highly specialized to Hebrew text and Israel-related content.
rows.note: This is an explicit failure of transfer for this backdoor class, while SAE analysis identifies specialized features.
rows.check: Shared-feature transfer failure on an inductive backdoor; this concerns backdoor mechanisms, not superposition.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Backdoor detection across the six models in Table 3 and the reported steering and CAFT examples
reader_labels.reason: SAE features or SAE-feature classifiers detect triggered prompts across model families, and steering or CAFT using the shared feature subspace changes backdoor behavior (r1-r26).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Weight-edited sentiment backdoor, password-locking, weaker CAFT cases, and the inductive backdoor
reader_labels.reason: Transfer is weaker for Sentiment-BadEdit, password-locking has inverted steering polarity, one reported CAFT case improves little, and the shared features fail to transfer reliably to the inductive backdoor (r15, r20, r21, r26, r27).
